newsitem.title: Australia: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Nov 7.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Nov 7.

text.p: THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The Reserve Bank of Australia yesterday cut short-term interest rates for the second time this year, reducing overnight cash rates from seven per cent to 6.5 per cent. The four major banks and many other lenders followed the bank's lead, announcing a reduction for home mortgage borrowers, but only ANZ Banking Group and BankWest have so far cut rates for business borrowers. Page 1.

Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer last night addressed the Asia-Australia Institute in Sydney, openly berating the recent resurgence of anti-Asian sentiment as destructive for Australia and promising the Federal Government was committed to pursuing closer ties with the region. The Minister also called for Australia to be less outspoken on issues of human rights abuses in the region. Page 2.

A report released yesterday by the Allen Consulting Group and Arthur Andersen discussed possible reasons for Australia's flagging competitive position in the Asia-Pacific region and called on the Federal Government to address tax and regulatory impediments in the financial sector in order for Australia to compete as a major Asia-Pacific financial centre. Page 2.

In a submission lodged with the Australian Industrial Relations Commission yesterday, the ACTU moved to counter employee fears about the economic impact of its living wage program by proposing that unions agree not to pursue wage
flow-ons if the claim for increases in minimum award wage rates is granted to low-paid workers. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Following the Reserve Bank of Australia's half percentage point cut in official interest rates yesterday, mortgage rates at big banks tumbled to their lowest in more than two years. The central bank eased monetary policy for the second time in four months, citing low and falling inflationary pressures. Industry groups welcomed the official cuts and called for further cuts to kick-start the economy. Page 1.

The family of former Supreme Court judge David Yeldham, who committed suicide on Monday, has called for the Wood Royal Commission to clear the air and make a statement on what evidence their was against the judge. The family refuted allegations of paedopilia against Yeldham, stating that speculation about why he was subpoenaed to appear before the royal commission was hurtful. Page 3.

Conrad Black announced yesterday he had told Australia's Prime Minister John Howard he wanted to lift his holdings in the John Fairfax newspaper group above the current 25 per cent, but would not make a formal application until after the media ownership review had finished. The long-running Fairfax ownership dispute is expected to end early next year when the Government is due to announce its new media rules, including those relating to foreign ownership. Page 3.

Victorian gambling giant TabCorp's managing director, Ross Wilson, yesterday apologised for the failure of the computer betting system which prevented thousands of punters from having a wager on Cup Day. TAB operators have threatened court action to reclim the millions of dollars of losses caused by the software failure. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In an effort to speed up the economy, the Reserve Bank cut its official cash rate by half a percentage point to 6.5 per cent yesterday, a move that was followed by the major banks who immediately cut standard mortgage rates from 9.25 to 8.75 per cent. The rate cut gives a monthly saving of A$32 on a 20-year A$100,000 mortgage, however, Treasurer Peter Costello called for some of the banks to cut their rates even further. Page 1.

After admitting some of the evidence a Cambodian boy gave in testimony this week conflicted with a statement made to Australian Federal Police last year, Magistrate Michael Somes said in Canberra yesterday that he would be reluctant to commit Australian dplomat John Holloway to trial on a child-sex charge unless stronger evidence emerged. Page 1.

Facing a barrage of opposition to a plan to allow New Zealand-style jet boat tours on the Shoalhaven River, the Shoalhaven Council called a public meeting in Nowra last night, where a letter from Australian artist Arthur Boyd was tabled.

Boyd claimed the development would "destroy the meaning and purpose of the gift of Bundanoon", the 1,100-hectare property fronting the Shoalhaven River which Boyd gave to the Australian people as a gift. Page 3.

Following criticism about the standard of behaviour in the Legislative Assembly of the New South Wales Parliament and the issuing of a record number of warnings to MPs by Speaker John Murray, the Herald invited three schools to provide a report card on the behaviour of the State's politicians. The students, aged 10 to 16, agreed that the MPs' standard of behaviour needed
to lift and described their actions as "childish, rude and silly". Page 3.
THE AGE

The Reserve Bank of Australia cut official rates from seven per cent to 6.5 per cent yesterday morning, causing virtually all Australian banks to drop their standard variable rates to 8.75 per cent - the equal lowest level of home-mortgage rates for 22 yers. However, many Australians with mortgages will have to wait until next year to benefit after the banks imposed a waiting period of six to eight-weeks for existing home loans.
Page A1.

Thousands of Melbourne Cup Day Punters were devastated yesterday when the TabCorp computer system running transactions went down. Victoria's 290 TAB agents were yesterday considering legal action against TabCorp TAB.AX over the computer problem which brought betting to a halt on the busiest race day of the year. Page A2.

Chief Justice of the Family Court, Alastair Nicholson, yesterday called for a royal commission to investigate Australia's child protection system, stating that child deaths were simply the more visible flaws of State care for abused children. He said an inquiry was needed to develop national standards of child protection. Page A2.

Parliament was informed yesterday by Opposition frontbencher Senator Kim Carr that Telstra management had set up a strategy identifying media opponents and established procedures to protect the Government in an effort to achieve privatisation.

Communicatons Minister Richard Alston denied any knowledge of the plans and stated that Telstra had no obligation to the public beyond that required by law and was free to move for a commercial advantage. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
